sentences.text: The genus Deltadromeus contains a single species, D. agilis, known only from an incomplete postcranial skeleton that lacks most vertebrae, ribs, and forelimbs.
Based on the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — Deltadromeus was approximately 8 meters long and weighed 1050 kilograms, a size estimate confirmed by Frank Seebacher in 2001.

Its tibia-to-femur length-to-diameter ratio is 0.95, which is higher than the 0.76 seen in Allosaurus but lower than the 1.16 found in Ornithomimus, and a 2025 study noted that it lacks a femoral crest, a trait seen in ornithomimids like Struthiomimus and Gallimimus.
Despite its size, Deltadromeus was a carnivore with unusually thin hind legs for its size, suggesting it was a fast runner.
Specimens from the Bahariya Formation suggest a much larger size, with one femur measuring 1.22 meters compared to the holotype's 0.741 meters.
Isotopic evidence suggests carcharodontosaurids and ceratosaurs in the Kem Kem Beds and Elrhaz Formation consumed sizable terrestrial animals.
The genus Deltadromeus was described by American paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues in 1996, and the species D. agilis was described by Sereno in that same year.

Fossils definitively assigned to Deltadromeus were discovered in 1996 by Paul Sereno during an expedition in the Kem Kem Beds of eastern Morocco, though Deltadromeus fossils were discovered in 1995 by Gabrielle Lyon during an expedition led by Paul Sereno in the Tegana Formation of Morocco.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as SGM-Din 2, was an incomplete postcranial skeleton found at a single site.
Researchers suggest niche partitioning occurred among theropods, with spinosaurids eating fish and other groups hunting herbivorous dinosaurs.

Abelisauroid affinities suggest Deltadromeus may have been omnivorous or herbivorous, and if omnivorous or herbivorous, Deltadromeus and Bahariasaurus may have filled a niche typically occupied by ornithischians.
If Deltadromeus is closely related to herbivorous or omnivorous ceratosaurs like Limusaurus, it may have been herbivorous or omnivorous.
The diet of Deltadromeus cannot be confirmed because no skull material has been found.
Originally classified as a basal coelurosaur related to Ornitholestes, this classification has been challenged by later studies.

Many studies since its description have considered Deltadromeus to be a ceratosaur, though researchers disagree on the specific type of ceratosaur it represents, and Deltadromeus is tentatively classified in the suborder Ceratosauria.
A 2016 analysis suggested Deltadromeus and Gualicho were sister taxa within the family Neovenatoridae.
Some subsequent studies classified Deltadromeus as a ceratosaur, though they did not include Gualicho in their analysis.

Sereno and others described Deltadromeus as a basal coelurosaurian in 1996, but Rauhut placed it within ornithomimosaurians, and the Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Deltadromeus as Noasauridae.

Fossils of Deltadromeus date to the Cenomanian stage of the Cretaceous period, approximately 100 to 95 million years ago, and Deltadromeus lived during the Cenomanian stage, from 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
Deltadromeus fossils are found in the Kem Kem Beds of North Africa, and Deltadromeus fossils are also found in the Bahariya Formation of Egypt and the Elrhaz and Echkar Formations of Niger.

During the Cretaceous, North Africa was covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, supporting diverse fish, crocodyliforms, and pterosaurs, and during the mid-Cretaceous, North Africa was a mangrove-dominated coastal environment with vast tidal flats and waterways bordering the Tethys Sea.

It is debated whether Deltadromeus and Bahariasaurus are distinct genera or if one is a synonym of the other, some studies suggest Deltadromeus may be a junior synonym of Bahariasaurus though this is not universally accepted, and it is debated whether Deltadromeus is a distinct genus or merely a synonym of the poorly understood dinosaur Bahariasaurus.
